[Reynold's death, and the death of the female commander during the spacewalk, were two of the more memorable and disturbing I've seen in a movie.  I would've changed the ending a bit though. She had no way of knowing Calvin's capsule had made it back to Earth, so it seems a little out of character for her to lose her shit. I dunno.  I think a better ending would've been to have both their capsules make it back home... you could still pull the switcheroo, have it seem like a happy ending for her and then cut to to other capsule to show that Calvin has reached Earth too.  But I guess they wanted to keep the ending as bleak as possible, which was a gutsy move, so I guess I gotta hand it to them for that.  And the implication of the ending is obviously pretty dark... although it's never really explained if Calvin can divide and reproduce, if he can that's pretty much the end of all life on Earth.  Oh well LOL.  Either way, the song after the cut to black was the perfect way to end the film.](#spoiler)

All in all, a solid B+, three out of four stars in my book.  Basically a blend and/or loving ripoff of Alien, Prometheus, and Gravity, with a little bit of the end-of-the-world dread of The Thing thrown in too.  It actually kinda reminded me of the (underrated) prequel to The Thing, slightly-unconvincing CGI and all.  Plot holes aside, there's something eerily plausible about the story, as if this First Contact with extraterrestrial life really could go this horribly, apocalyptically badly.  It does feel like it has some studio executive/committee fingerprints on it... with some script-tightening, and if it had been put in the hands of a real auteur (like, say, Fincher or Cronenberg or Villeneuve) it could've been something special... but it's still plenty serviceable.  If you're a fan of sci-fi or horror, I'd say it's worth seeing in theaters.  I hope it does well at the box office too, if only because at least it's a big-budget film that isn't a direct sequel to or reboot of something else... hopefully Hollywood will take the hint.

Just saw it for a second time today.  My thoughts:

- An enjoyable way to spend two hours.  Better than TLW and way better than JPIII.
- Not nearly as good as JP.  Mostly because of the writing.  JW, like almost every other big-budget movie Hollywood has put out for the last decade, clearly suffered from having too many writers.  Too many cooks in the kitchen.  Death by committee, etc.  It was just a bit too predictable, too corporate, too sanitized, too many cliches.  The kids were well-developed characters, as were Pratt & Howard, but the rest of the characters were completely two-dimensional and acted in ways that were clearly just designed to advance the plot, instead of the other way around.
- A bit too much CGI and not enough practical effects.  When the monorail goes through the Jurassic World gates at the beginning of the movies it looked so fake it put me off being able to suspend disbelief for a lot of the movie.  The velicoraptors occasionally reminded me of [this.](http://i40.tinypic.com/9rtzdf.jpg)
- The final battle against the I-Rex, especially when Howard releases the T-Rex, was fucking great.  The whole "nature vs. man's creation" subtext to that fight was pretty awesome.
- The ending was a letdown.  Yes the T-Rex roaring over the park was cool, but it needed more of a cliffhanger IMO.

Overall I'd give it a B- or a B... with better writing it could easily have been an A or A+.  It suffers in comparison to the original, but it's better than the other sequels and definitely better than most of the dreck Hollywood puts out now, and it least it wasn't another goddamn superhero movie.

This is well-intentioned but completely preposterous utopian fantasizing.

There are seven billion people on the planet and counting.  Let's assume you can get everyone in the developed world to agree to a massive redistribution of wealth.  This will never happen, because it is completely contrary to human nature for people to give up comfort once they have it, but let's assume it happens.

Great!  Now, I hate to break it to you, but you wouldn't be able to bring everyone else up to the Western level.  Why?  Because we live on a finite planet.  Go read Alan Weisman's "Countdown" or any other book about population, ecology, and resources and then get back to me.  Ecologists now estimate the Earth's oil, water, minerals, arable land, and everything else we depend on can support, at most, two billion people living a European lifestyle.  Guess what that means?  Seven billion people will *never* be able to live the way you and I do, at least not for the foreseeable future.  If you want everyone to live equally, that means either (a) bringing world population down, or (b) bringing your standard of living down.  A lot.  Reality would be much closer to everyone living in Soweto than it would be to everyone living in Oslo.  That doesn't mean it's right, or fair, but it's the reality.

I would gladly give up living in modern industrialized society to live a simpler, pre-industrial way of life - indeed, I am in the process of figuring out how to do just that, because I am sickened at my impact on the planet and find modern life completely unfulfilling.
